name: The Forest and Tower of Wayreth

pages.name: The Forest
pages.html:
You do not travel to Wayreth. You are admitted to it, or you are not, and the distinction is not yours to make.

The Forest of Wayreth occupies a stretch of the far south of Ansalon, below the Plains of Dust, in country nobody has any other reason to visit. Cartographers place it differently on every map, and every one of them is correct on the day it was drawn.

The trees are old. Not ancient in the picturesque sense — old in the way that stone is old, with the same indifference. They are pale-barked, close-grown, and they do not move while anyone is looking at them.

Finding It

There is no navigation check that finds Wayreth. Say this to the players plainly the first time they try, because the instinct to roll Survival is overwhelming and letting them roll implies a target number exists.

What determines admission:

ConditionResult
Summoned by the ConclaveAdmitted. The path is short and obvious.
Carrying business the Tower wantsAdmitted, by a longer route, and observed the whole way.
Seeking it with no businessRefused. The party emerges on open moorland facing the direction they came from, having lost between one and six days they cannot account for.
Hostile intentRefused, and the forest is no longer neutral. See The Refused.
Not looking for it at allOccasionally admitted anyway. This is the one that frightens the Conclave.

Running the Journey

Play the forest as a corridor, not a wilderness. Once inside, the party has no meaningful navigational choices — the path exists, it goes one way, and stepping off it puts them back on it a few minutes later facing the same direction.

Give them three or four beats on the walk and make each one an observation rather than an obstacle:

  • The light does not change. It has been the same hour since they entered.
  • They pass a milestone carved with a name. Hours later, they pass it again. The name is different.
  • Someone hears a conversation they had years ago, at conversational volume, from just off the path.
  • A tree has a door in it. It is closed. It is not locked.

None of these should be resolvable. The forest is not a puzzle and there is nothing to solve; it is establishing, before the party ever reaches the Tower, that they are somewhere with its own opinions.

DM Note

Everything on this page is the forest making decisions. Not the Conclave, and not the wards — the forest. The party should be able to reconstruct this eventually from three or four observations, well before anyone tells them.

The strongest version: the party is admitted once on Conclave business and once when they were going somewhere else entirely. The second time is when a clever player says wait.

pages.name: The Refused
pages.html:
The forest does not kill trespassers. It is more patient than that, and the results are worse.

Those who force the issue — who press on after being turned, who arrive with fire and intent — find that the forest simply stops ending. Not a maze; a maze has a solution. The path continues and continues and the light does not change and eventually they sit down.

Mechanics: Refusal

A creature the forest has refused, which persists in entering, is subject to the following at the end of each hour spent within the treeline:

DC 15 Wisdom saving throw. On a failure, the creature gains one level of exhaustion and cannot remove it by resting while it remains in the forest. On a success, no effect, but the DC increases by 1 for each subsequent hour.

Magical travel does not help. Teleport, dimension door, plane shift, and similar effects fail while within the treeline unless cast by a creature the forest has admitted. Attempts are not merely wasted — the caster takes 4d6 psychic damage and learns, with certainty and without words, that it was noticed.

A creature reduced to six levels of exhaustion by the forest does not die. It is set down on the moor, alive, at the treeline. It has no memory of the attempt and cannot be made to have one. Whatever it came to do, it no longer wants to.

The Ones Still In There

Not everyone gets set down. Perhaps a dozen figures walk the forest permanently — wizards, mostly, from various centuries, who came for the Tower and were neither admitted nor released.

They are not hostile and not undead. They are lost in the specific sense that the forest has declined to conclude their business. They will speak to the party, helpfully, at length, and their information is accurate as of whichever century they entered.

One of them can be persuaded to walk with the party. This is not a good idea, and the forest permits it, which should worry anyone paying attention.

pages.name: The Approach and the Gate
pages.html:
The forest ends without warning — not thinning, just ending, at the edge of a clearing perhaps a quarter-mile across. The grass is short and the ground is level and nothing grows in it.

The Tower stands in the centre. It is not one tower. Two spires of black stone rise on either side of a central keep, and the whole structure is windowless for its lower two-thirds, and the stone drinks light in a way that makes it difficult to judge distance or height. Most visitors substantially underestimate both.

The Gate

A single gate of dark iron, unguarded, unlocked, and standing open.

This is deliberate and it is the Tower's first real test of anyone who reaches the clearing. There is nothing to defeat, nothing to pick, no one to talk past. The party must simply decide to walk in, and the Tower makes that decision as difficult as possible by removing every excuse for delay.

Optional: a first-time visitor crossing the clearing may make a DC 13 Wisdom (Perception) check. On a success, they notice that they have been walking toward the gate for considerably longer than a quarter-mile warrants, and that they are not tired.

Rules of Conduct

A plaque inside the gate, in Common, Solamnic, Elvish, Dwarvish, and three scripts nobody present will recognise. It is short:

Draw no weapon. Cast no spell you have not declared. Open no door that is closed to you. Take nothing.

You are a guest of the Tower and not of its Master. Address your grievances accordingly.

These are enforced, and the enforcement is not subtle.

ViolationResponse
Weapon drawnThe weapon becomes too heavy to lift (Strength save DC 18 to hold, and it cannot be swung). Effect ends when sheathed.
Undeclared spellThe spell functions. The caster then takes psychic damage equal to twice the slot level in d6, and every resident of the Tower knows what was cast and where.
Forcing a closed doorThe corridor lengthens. The party walks for ten minutes and arrives back at the entrance hall.
TheftThe item cannot leave the building. Neither, until it is returned, can the thief.

Note the last line of the plaque. The Tower distinguishes between itself and its Master, in writing, on a plaque that predates him by three hundred years. Attentive players will notice.

pages.name: Inside: The Public Tower
pages.html:
Wayreth is larger inside than the clearing allows. Nobody discusses this.

The Hall of Mages

The entrance hall, and the only room most visitors ever see. Black stone, no windows, lit by cold silver flames in sconces that produce no heat. Twenty-one chairs in a wide arc — seven of white marble, seven of red porphyry, seven of black basalt — facing a single seat on a low dais.

The Conclave sits here. When it is not sitting, the chairs are still there, and the room is still lit, and the effect on a party waiting for an audience is exactly as intended.

The dais seat is the Master's. It is currently occupied more often than it has been in living memory, because Raistlin conducts business from it rather than from a study, and the White Robes have not worked out whether that is a statement or simply the most convenient chair.

The Guest Range

West spire, lower floors. Plain, comfortable, and scrupulously well-appointed — the Tower is a courteous host. Rooms have no locks, on the stated principle that a guest of the Tower requires no protection from it. Several guests have observed that this principle has an obvious second reading.

The Libraries

Three, on ascending floors of the central keep, and access is by robe.

  • The Open Library. Any guest. General arcana, history, geography, several thousand volumes of Conclave minutes that no one has ever read voluntarily.
  • The Second Library. Wizards of High Sorcery only — that is, those who have passed the Test. A PC gains access the day they pass, and it should feel like a genuine reward. Spell research, planar cosmology, the Orders' working records.
  • The Sealed Library. Conclave members and the Master. Contains the surviving records of the four fallen Towers, the full account of the Lost Battles, and the Conclave's private history of its own conduct during them.

DM Note — The Sealed Library

What is in there that the Conclave will not discuss: the minutes of the negotiation with the Kingpriest, unedited. They show that the terms offered by Istar were considerably better than the terms accepted, and that the Conclave took the worse deal in order to keep the Black Robes seated.

Three centuries of institutional guilt rest on a decision that was, on the evidence, morally correct and strategically catastrophic. Par-Salian has read it. Raistlin has read it. It is the reason Raistlin's argument landed.

The Refectory and the Yard

Sixty residents have to eat. The refectory is the one room in Wayreth that feels like a building rather than an institution, and it is by far the best place to run NPC scenes. Apprentices gossip. Red Robes argue. The food is good, which surprises everybody.

pages.name: Daily Life Behind the Wards
pages.html:
Wayreth is a wonder of the world occupied by people who still need clean linen, lamp oil, quiet places to quarrel, and someone willing to repair the roof after an apprentice animates the rain.

The Household

Roughly sixty people reside in the Tower during ordinary months: twenty-five robed wizards, twelve apprentices, eight librarians and copyists, six kitchen and household staff, three wardens, two healers, and several guests whose departure dates have become theoretical. The Tower creates space but not labor. Residents serve rotations regardless of rank, though senior Black Robes have developed astonishing interpretations of what counts as pantry duty.

A Typical Day

  • Dawn: moon observations are entered into the common ledger; overnight experiments are inspected; apprentices eat before their mentors.
  • Morning: instruction, correspondence, library work, and public audiences. Undeclared casting is forbidden in shared rooms.
  • Midday: the refectory meal is the only gathering not organized by robe. Seating by Order is considered embarrassingly provincial.
  • Afternoon: laboratories open, petitioners are received, and supervised candidates practice in the warded yard.
  • Moonrise: each Order holds observance privately. Red Robes welcome guests; White Robes sometimes do; Black Robes deny an observance occurred.
  • Night: the libraries remain open. Corridors rearrange to shorten the route for anyone carrying too many books.

Customs Visitors Learn Late

Never ask what happened in another wizard's Test. Never touch a robe hanging without its owner. Leave a laboratory door exactly as found. A book placed spine-inward is under dispute and may not be cited. When all conversation stops in the refectory, the Master has entered even if nobody can see him.

Rumors in Residence

d6RumorTruth
1The west stair adds a step for every lie told upon it.False, but three apprentices are counting.
2Raistlin dismissed his own reflection from the mirrors.Mirrors show him; one particular mirror refuses.
3A sealed room contains a living dragon egg.True, and it has begun dreaming.
4Justarius cheats at stones.True, openly, and nobody knows how.
5The forest attends Conclave meetings.Not as a person.
6Someone has been removing names from the guest ledger.True. The removed guests have not left.

pages.name: Gazetteer of the Inner Tower
pages.html:
Use these rooms as destinations, discoveries, or the scene the Tower chooses when a corridor needs to end somewhere inconvenient.

PlaceAppearanceUse in play
Hall of MagesTwenty-one colored seats and the Master's low dais.Votes, trials, formal accusations, and silences with witnesses.
Moon CourtAn open court whose sky remains visible through every weather.Sanction rites; the stones mark all three lunar paths.
ScriptoriumLong desks, blue lamps, dry air, no shadows.Research scenes; a copied error points to deliberate falsification.
Hall of ApprenticesSmall rooms around a warm common chamber.Gossip, rivalry, missing student, or an invitation delivered at midnight.
RefectoryPlain oak tables and excellent bread.Neutral social ground where enemies must share salt.
InfirmaryWhite tile, herb cabinets, three beds behind black curtains.Marks from failed magic; evidence of Raistlin's private treatments.
Chamber of SeeingBlack basin beneath a ceiling of moving stars.Scrying that reveals what matters instead of what was requested.
Room of MeasuresScales, rods, clocks, sealed weights.Identify unstable magic; discover an item growing heavier each night.
Names GalleryStone panels bearing every tested wizard.A name has appeared years before its owner is born.
Hall of DoorsTwelve freestanding doors in a circular room.Controlled transit; one opens onto a fallen Tower for seven breaths.
Quiet CryptMemorial niches without bodies.Speak with an archive-echo; learn which histories were edited.
Deep CatalogueIron lecterns above a shaft descending beyond sight.Vault index; removing a card causes the indexed object to stir.

Mutable Geography

Do not map every corridor. Give each important room a fixed relationship to two others and let the Tower control the rest. The refectory is always below the libraries. The Hall of Mages is always reached from the gate. The vaults are always down. Everything else may move when doing so reveals preference, protects a secret, or forces two people into the same scene.

pages.name: Inside: The Working Tower
pages.html:
Above the libraries, access stops being a matter of courtesy.

The Laboratories

East spire, upper floors. Individually warded, individually owned, and the Tower enforces those wards without reference to anyone's rank. A Conclave member cannot enter another's laboratory uninvited. Neither can the Master, which is one of the few structural checks on Raistlin's authority and is mentioned rather often by people trying to reassure themselves.

Notable occupants:

  • Justarius keeps a laboratory that is conspicuously untidy and conspicuously unwarded, and has never had anything taken from it.
  • Ladonna keeps two. One is a working laboratory. The other is not, and its contents are the subject of a standing Conclave motion that never quite comes to a vote.
  • The Master's laboratory is at the top of the east spire and the stair to it does not always exist.

The Chamber of Seeing

Central keep, high floor. A circular room containing a single basin of still black water, used for the Orders' scrying and for anchoring the Test's demiplane.

The basin shows what the Tower chooses rather than what the viewer asks for, about one time in five. This is documented as a known fault. It has never been repaired, because nobody has been able to identify what is faulty.

The Testing Chamber

There is no testing chamber.

The Test occupies a demiplane anchored to the Tower, and candidates enter from wherever they happen to be standing when the Master decides they are ready. Apprentices spend a great deal of time speculating about where the chamber is, and senior mages let them, because the answer — that it is everywhere, and that you are standing in it — is not calming.

The Vaults

Below the foundations. Everything reclaimed from Daltigoth, Losarcum, Istar, and Palanthas before the fall; everything confiscated from renegades in three hundred years; everything the Conclave has judged too dangerous to destroy, which is a category that requires some explaining to visitors.

Access is by the Master alone. Under the previous administration this was a formality, because Par-Salian went down perhaps twice a year and always with witnesses.

Raistlin goes down most nights, and takes no one.

DM Note — The Vaults

What he is doing depends on which agenda you chose in The Black Master of Wayreth.

  • Palanthas: he is looking for anything that survived the fall of the Palanthian Tower — keys, wards, records of the Curse's exact wording.
  • The Balance: he is arming third parties. Items leave the vault and turn up in the north, and the inventory is immaculate because he is falsifying it himself.
  • Survival: he is looking for a cure and there isn't one, and he has been down there most nights for four months.

If the party gets into the vaults — and the vaults are a very good third-act location — what they find there should tell them which of these is true, without a word of explanation.

pages.name: Defenses of the Last Tower
pages.html:
Wayreth's defenses were designed by people who expected armies, dragons, hostile archmages, and their own successors. They do not begin with damage.

Layers of Refusal

  1. Distance. The forest prevents hostile forces from finding the clearing. An army may march for weeks and emerge behind its own supply train.
  2. Intention. The clearing lengthens under anyone preparing violence. Charges fail because the gate recedes at walking pace.
  3. Disarmament. Weapons become burdens; siege engines forget their tension; fire burns fuel without spreading.
  4. Division. Intruders are routed into separate corridors tailored to their purpose. Commanders lose messengers before soldiers lose lives.
  5. Containment. Rooms seal, magic is grounded into foundation stones, and the Tower waits for surrender.
  6. Judgment. Only when the earlier layers fail do the guardian manifestations appear.

Emergency States

StateTriggerEffect
SilverUnidentified magic crosses the forest.Residents are notified; guest routes narrow; scrying turns outward.
RedA ward is attacked or a forbidden gate opens.Apprentices shelter; laboratories seal; the three Heads assemble.
BlackThe Tower's continuity is threatened.Vaults descend, libraries partition into demiplanes, and the forest moves the entire clearing.

Guardian Manifestations

The Tower prefers forms drawn from an intruder's understanding: an armored examiner, a dead mentor, a dragon made of script, or the intruder at the end of the path they have chosen. Use an appropriate CR 10–15 creature, change its damage to force or psychic, grant truesight 60 feet, and let it move through the Tower's stone. When reduced to 0 hit points it discorporates and reforms at the next moonrise.

DM Note — The Unthinkable Assault

The Dragonarmy cannot storm Wayreth by numbers. It can threaten the Tower only with corrupted dragon eggs, a captured invitation, an insider who sincerely believes opening the gate will preserve magic, or a weapon aimed at the forest's purpose rather than its trees. Build any assault around a moral breach. The walls are the least interesting thing to overcome.
